title: Module Documentation: k-Way Birthday Coincidences
content:
The module documentation outlines the four main results of this formalization: (1) the generalized pigeonhole bound — $n > (k-1)d$ forces a k-way coincidence; (2) classical recovery — the $k=2$ case is equivalent to non-injectivity; (3) monotonicity — stronger coincidences imply weaker ones; (4) probability = 1 when the pigeonhole bound is exceeded. The approach uses Mathlib's `Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise` for fiber decomposition and `Finset.sum_le_sum` for bounding.

The historical note records the scaling of thresholds: for $d = 365$ days, $k=2$ needs ~23 people (the classical surprise), $k=3$ needs ~88, and $k=4$ needs ~187. The general scaling is $d^{(k-1)/k} \cdot (k!)^{1/k}$.
mathContext: Threshold for $>50\%$ probability of a k-way coincidence among $d$ equally likely outcomes: $n \approx d^{(k-1)/k} \cdot (k!)^{1/k}$. For $d=365$: $n_2 \approx 23$, $n_3 \approx 88$, $n_4 \approx 187$.

title: Fiber Definition: People Assigned to a Day
content:
The fiber `fiberAt f j` is the set of people assigned to day `j` by the birthday assignment `f`. Formally, it filters `Finset.univ` (all people) by the predicate `f i = j`. This is the fundamental building block: a k-way coincidence occurs when some fiber has cardinality at least `k`.

The fiber perspective converts a problem about functions into a problem about set cardinalities, enabling the use of Mathlib's powerful `Finset` API for counting arguments.

title: HasKWay: The k-Way Coincidence Predicate
content:
A k-way coincidence occurs when some day `j` has at least `k` people assigned to it: $\exists j, k \leq |\text{fiberAt}(f, j)|$. This existential definition is clean and enables both the pigeonhole proof (by contradiction on the negation) and the probability framework (by counting assignments satisfying the predicate).

Note the direction: `k ≤ card` rather than `card ≥ k`. This is idiomatic in Mathlib, where `≤` is the preferred relation.

title: Fiber Partition of Unity
content:
The fiber sizes sum to $n$: $\sum_{j \in \text{Fin}\,d} |\text{fiberAt}(f, j)| = n$. This is the partition-of-unity identity — every person belongs to exactly one fiber (the day they're assigned to), so summing over fibers counts each person exactly once.

The proof applies Mathlib's `Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise`, which expresses $|S| = \sum_{t \in T} |\{s \in S \mid f(s) = t\}|$ for any function $f : S \to T$. The `simp` and `linarith` close the goal after specializing to `S = \text{Fin}\,n$, $T = \text{Fin}\,d$.
mathContext: $\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} |\text{fiberAt}(f, j)| = n$, since the fibers $\{f^{-1}(j)\}_{j \in \text{Fin}\,d}$ partition $\text{Fin}\,n$.

title: Generalized Pigeonhole for Birthdays
content:
The central result: if $n > (k-1) \cdot d$, then every birthday assignment has a k-way coincidence. The proof proceeds by contradiction: assume every fiber has fewer than $k$ elements (i.e., $|\text{fiberAt}(f, j)| < k$ for all $j$). Then each fiber has $\leq k-1$ elements, so $n = \sum_j |\text{fiberAt}(f, j)| \leq \sum_j (k-1) = (k-1) \cdot d < n$, a contradiction.

The `calc` block makes the reasoning explicit: `Finset.sum_le_sum` lifts the pointwise bound, `Finset.sum_const` evaluates the constant sum, and `omega` closes the final arithmetic contradiction.

title: Concrete Pigeonhole Instances for d=365
content:
Three concrete examples instantiate the generalized pigeonhole for the standard 365-day calendar:
- `pigeonhole_365`: general template for any $k$ with $d=365$
- $k=2$: 366 people guarantee a pairwise collision ($365 \cdot 1 < 366$) — the classical pigeonhole
- $k=3$: 731 people guarantee a triple collision ($365 \cdot 2 < 731$)

These serve as sanity checks: the pigeonhole bound $(k-1) \cdot 365$ gives the hard threshold. The real surprise of the birthday problem is that the *probabilistic* threshold (>50% chance) is much lower than the pigeonhole (certainty) threshold.
mathContext:
$k=2$: $n > 365$ guarantees a collision (pigeonhole), but $n \ge 23$ gives $>50\%$ probability.
$k=3$: $n > 730$ guarantees a triple, but $n \ge 88$ gives $>50\%$ probability.

title: Classical Recovery: 2-Way = Non-Injective
content:
Proves the equivalence `HasKWay f 2 ↔ ¬Function.Injective f`. Forward: a fiber with $\ge 2$ elements gives two distinct people $i_1 \neq i_2$ with $f(i_1) = f(i_2) = j$, contradicting injectivity. The key step uses `Finset.one_lt_card` to extract the two distinct witnesses. Backward: non-injectivity gives $f(i_1) = f(i_2)$ with $i_1 \neq i_2$, so the fiber at $f(i_1)$ contains both $i_1$ and $i_2$, giving $|\text{fiber}| \geq 2$.

This equivalence is the bridge between the k-way framework and the original birthday problem, which is typically stated in terms of injectivity (all birthdays distinct).
mathContext:
$\text{HasKWay}(f, 2) \iff \neg\text{Injective}(f)$

Equivalently: $\exists j,\; |f^{-1}(j)| \ge 2 \iff \exists i_1 \ne i_2,\; f(i_1) = f(i_2)$

title: Monotonicity in k
content:
Two monotonicity results: (1) `hasKWay_mono`: a k-way coincidence implies a $k'$-way coincidence for $k' \leq k$ — if some day has $\geq k$ people, it certainly has $\geq k'$ people. The proof is a simple `le_trans`. (2) `hasKWay_implies_pair`: specializes to $k' = 2$, formalizing 'a birthday triple implies a birthday pair.'

These capture the intuitive ordering: stronger coincidences imply weaker ones.
mathContext: $k' \le k \text{ and } \exists j,\; |f^{-1}(j)| \ge k \implies \exists j,\; |f^{-1}(j)| \ge k'$

title: Probability Framework: noKWaySet and probKWay
content:
`noKWaySet n d k` is the set of birthday assignments where every day has fewer than $k$ people — the 'safe' assignments. `probKWay n d k` is defined as $1 - |\text{noKWaySet}| / d^n$, following the standard complementary counting approach: the probability of a k-way coincidence equals 1 minus the probability of avoiding one.

The definition is `noncomputable` because it involves division in $\mathbb{Q}$ computed from a finite set cardinality — the computation is well-defined but Lean's kernel can't evaluate it.

title: Probability = 1 Under Pigeonhole
content: When $n > (k-1) \cdot d$, the probability of a k-way coincidence is exactly 1: every possible birthday assignment has a k-way coincidence, so `noKWaySet` is empty. The proof shows `noKWaySet n d k = ∅` by deriving a contradiction for any hypothetical member using `pigeonhole_kway`, then `simp` computes $1 - 0/d^n = 1$.

title: Probability Monotonicity: noKWaySet and probKWay
content:
`noKWaySet_mono` proves set containment: $k' \leq k \implies \text{noKWaySet}(n, d, k') \subseteq \text{noKWaySet}(n, d, k)$. Avoiding a $k'$-way coincidence is a stronger condition than avoiding a $k$-way one (every fiber has $< k'$ elements implies $< k$ elements).

`probKWay_mono_k` converts set containment into probability ordering: $k' \leq k \implies P(\text{k-way}) \leq P(\text{k'-way})$. Higher-order coincidences are harder to achieve, so their probability is lower. The proof uses `div_le_div_of_nonneg_right` on the cardinalities.
mathContext:
$k' \le k \implies P(\text{k-way coincidence}) \le P(\text{k'-way coincidence})$

Equivalently: it is harder to find $k$ people sharing a birthday than $k' < k$ people.

title: noKWaySet for k=2 Equals Injective Functions
content:
For $k=2$, the set of assignments with no k-way coincidence is exactly the set of injective functions. This bridges the general probability framework to the classical birthday formula: $P(\text{no collision}) = \frac{d!/(d-n)!}{d^n} = \frac{d}{d} \cdot \frac{d-1}{d} \cdots \frac{d-n+1}{d}$.

The proof delegates to `no_kway_two_iff_injective`, converting between the fiber-based and function-based characterizations.

title: No k-Way When n < k, and Probability = 0
content:
`no_kway_of_lt`: When $n < k$, no assignment can have a k-way coincidence — you can't have $k$ people at one birthday with fewer than $k$ people total. The proof bounds $|\text{fiberAt}(f, j)| \leq |\text{Fin}\,n| = n < k$.

`probKWay_zero_of_lt`: The probability is 0 when $n < k$, since every assignment avoids k-way coincidences: $\text{noKWaySet} = \text{univ}$, so $P = 1 - d^n/d^n = 0$. The proof uses `div_self` to evaluate $d^n / d^n = 1$.

Together with `probKWay_one_of_pigeonhole`, these bracket the probability: $P = 0$ for $n < k$, $P = 1$ for $n > (k-1)d$, and $0 < P < 1$ in between.
mathContext:
$n < k \implies P(\text{k-way}) = 0$ and $n > (k-1)d \implies P(\text{k-way}) = 1$.

The interesting regime is $k \le n \le (k-1)d$ where $0 < P < 1$.
